power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Power also improved with increases in sample size: at the smallest sample size combination, average power across conditions was 48.92%, whereas at the largest sample size combination, average power was 87.70%. Across all conditions, the average power was 75.44%. Bauer et al. (2006) reported that the MC method resulted in slightly superior power rates than the NA method and that these differences were small. We observed a similar pattern, with the MC method producing slightly higher power than the NA method. Indeed, out of all the possible comparisons in Figure 7, the MC method outperformed the NA method in 108/216 cases, performed equally to the NA method in 94/216 cases, and performed worse than the NA method in only 14/216 cases. Collapsed across all conditions, the average power under the MC method was 75.82%, compared to 75.06% for the NA method.

We assessed convergence rates under different simulation conditions and the bias of the indirect effect and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 estimates. Then, we compared the performance of both indirect effect CI methods in terms of Type I error rates, CI coverage, and power. Convergence was considered successful when the optimizer returned a convergence code of 0, the Hessian matrix was positive definite, the smallest eigenvalue of the estimated covariance matrix was positive, and both the asymptotic normal approximation and Monte Carlo CIs could be computed. Bias was computed as the difference between the mean estimate across all replications within a given condition and the corresponding true population value. The Type I error rate was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs for the average indirect effect failed to contain zero under conditions where the indirect effect was null. We compared the observed Type I error rate to the nominal alpha level of 0.05. Coverage was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs contained the true value of the indirect effect. Note that Type I error and coverage are redundant in null conditions. As a benchmark, coverage and Type I error also used Bradley's liberal criterion (Bradley, 1978): For a nominal alpha level of 5%, acceptable Type I error rates should fall between 2.5% and 7.5%, and for 95% coverage, between 92.5% and 97.5%. Power was calculated for the main design cells where the true indirect effect was not zero.

info.title: Computationally efficient interval estimation for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R: A replication of Bauer, Preacher, and Gil (2006)

text.text: developed a popular estimation approach for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, using simulations to evaluate the performance of two computationally efficient ways to obtain intervals for the indirect effect.
While the model can be estimated in a variety of software packages, support in R lags behind as the original approaches to interval estimation were demonstrated using commercial software.
Recent research with R instead has only demonstrated interval estimation with more computationally intensive methods.
Meanwhile, other recent work has focused attention towards how Monte Carlo simulation studies are conducted and reported, highlighting the importance of replicating previous findings.
Our goals in this manuscript are twofold.

First, we show how to implement the original computationally efficient interval estimation methods for the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model in R. We do so by using the Delta method to obtain elements of the asymptotic covariance matrix among model parameters necessary for these approaches.
Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate and extend the original simulation study by Bauer et al. (2006).
text.formatted: Second, in a pre-registered study, we evaluate our implementation by attempting to partially replicate and extend the original simulation study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bauer et al. (2006)</ref>.

text.text: In general, our results indicate that our implementation is operating as expected as Type I error rates and coverage were acceptable when assumptions were met.
Furthermore, though we observed higher convergence rates, the major findings from Bauer et al. (2006) were replicated.

text.text: We hope that extensions to this work will help lead to more advanced multilevel mediation analysis models being readily available to applied researchers.

For estimating indirect effects with nested data where all variables are manipulated or measured at the lowest level, the 1-1-1 mediation analysis model is a well-known solution (Krull & MacKinnon, 2001).

Performing inference or interval estimation for the indirect effect typically requires some way of approximating its sampling distribution.

text.text: The asymptotic normal approximation results as a byproduct of using maximum likelihood estimation.
The indirect effect is a function of the maximum likelihood estimates of other model parameters.

As such, its sampling distribution can also be assumed asymptotically normal and an estimate of its sampling variance can be obtained from elements of an estimate of the so-called asymptotic covariance matrix (ACM) of the model parameters.

In brief, the ACM is a q by q matrix, 𝛀, where q is the number of model parameters (e.g., including fixed effect estimates, Level 1 error variances, and random effect variances and covariances); the diagonals of this matrix provide the sampling variability (and their square roots, standard errors) for all model parameters.
Across repeated samples, parameter estimates may also tend to co-vary.

Thus, the off-diagonal elements are the covariances among model parameters. Bauer et al. (2006) derive an estimate of the sampling variability of the indirect effect by use of a second-order Delta method in conjunction with elements from 𝛀 (p. 147; Eq 9), which under our notation is:

In practice, sample estimates of the parameters (𝑎 ̂1 and 𝑏 ̂2) are substituted into (10) as are elements of an estimated ACM, 𝛀 ̂, yielding, 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑏 ̂2), 𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), and 𝐶𝑜𝑣 ̂(𝑎 ̂1, 𝑏 ̂2).
The square root of an estimate of (10), 𝑠𝑒 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) = √𝑉𝑎𝑟 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ), can then be used to form a confidence interval (CI) for the indirect effect.
For example, a 95% CI is formed by: (𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ) ± 1.96 × 𝑠𝑒 ̂(𝑎 ̂1𝑏 ̂2 + 𝜎 ̂𝑢1𝑗 ,𝑣 2𝑗 ).

text.text: Some conditions included a non-null indirect effect, while others included a null indirect effect in order to test Type I error rates.

Within non-null conditions, the simulation study followed a fully factorial design, consisting of 4 (Level 2 sample size) x 3 (Level 1 sample size) x 2 (Magnitude of fixed effects 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 ) x 3 (Magnitude of 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 ) x 3 (Distribution of 𝑢 1𝑗 and 𝑣 2𝑗 ), resulting in 216 non-null simulation conditions (Table 1).

text.text: The first two factors manipulated sample size by varying either the number of Level 2 units (𝑛2 = 25, 50, 100, or 200) or Level 1 units per cluster (𝑛1 = 4, 8, or 16).
The next two factors manipulated the size of the indirect effect by varying either 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 or 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 , which we will describe shortly.

In addition to the non-null conditions above, we included additional null conditions designed to test Type I error rates, in which the magnitudes of 𝑎 1 , 𝑏 2 , and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 were fixed to 0, but in which we fully crossed 4 (Level 2 sample size) x 3 (Level 1 sample size) x 3 (distributional conditions) in the same manner as in non-null conditions, resulting in 36 null conditions.

text.text: We assessed convergence rates under different simulation conditions and the bias of the indirect effect and 𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 estimates.
Then, we compared the performance of both indirect effect CI methods in terms of Type I error rates, CI coverage, and power.

Convergence was considered successful when the optimizer returned a convergence code of 0, the Hessian matrix was positive definite, the smallest eigenvalue of the estimated covariance matrix was positive, and both the asymptotic normal approximation and Monte Carlo CIs could be computed.
Bias was computed as the difference between the mean estimate across all replications within a given condition and the corresponding true population value.
The Type I error rate was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs for the average indirect effect failed to contain zero under conditions where the indirect effect was null.
We compared the observed Type I error rate to the nominal alpha level of 0.05.
Coverage was computed as the proportion of replications in which the 95% CIs contained the true value of the indirect effect.
Note that Type I error and coverage are redundant in null conditions.

As a benchmark, coverage and Type I error also used Bradley's liberal criterion (Bradley, 1978): For a nominal alpha level of 5%, acceptable Type I error rates should fall between 2.5% and 7.5%, and for 95% coverage, between 92.5% and 97.5%.

text.text: Overall, the NA method and the MC method both produced coverage rates close to the nominal rate when the random effects were normally distributed.

However, both methods experienced difficulty producing robust coverage rates when the random effects were nonnormally distributed, especially when the covariance was positive and, to a lesser extent, when it was negative.
These difficulties did not emerge when the covariance was zero.
Indeed, when the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was positive, all 96 cells in that section of the design fell below Bradley's lower limit of 92.5% coverage.
When the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was negative, 36/96 of the cells exhibited undercoverage and fell below Bradley's lower limit.

In contrast, when the random effects were nonnormal and the covariance was zero, only 7/96 of the cells fell outside Bradley's range, including six cases of under-coverage and one case of over-coverage, all occurring at the smallest Level 2 sample size of 25.

Finally, regardless of the covariance value, when the random effects were normally distributed, only 3/144 cells were outside of Bradley's criterion, including one case of under-coverage and two cases of over-coverage, all at 𝑛2 = 25.

Indeed, when the magnitude of the true indirect effect was at its smallest (𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 = -0.113 and 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.3), power ranged from 1.87% to 28.35%.
In contrast, when the magnitude of the true indirect effect was at its largest (𝜎 𝑢 1𝑗 𝑣 2𝑗 = 0.113 and 𝑎1 = 𝑏2 = 0.6), power ranged from 94.34% to 100.00%.

Power also improved with increases in sample size: at the smallest sample size combination, average power across conditions was 48.92%, whereas at the largest sample size combination, average power was 87.70%.

Our simulation study had two main goals.

First, we aimed to test whether estimating the model using glmmTMB (McGillycuddy et al., 2025) and custom R code for the Delta method to obtain the asymptotic covariance between random effects 𝑎 1 and 𝑏 2 could be used to produce confidence intervals for the indirect effect in the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation model.

text.text: This goal was achieved: our study produced reasonable results across the examined performance measures.

Indeed, we obtained high convergence rates; our estimates were largely unbiased; the Type I error rate was often close to the nominal rate, particularly with the Monte Carlo method at larger sample sizes; and power to detect the indirect effect was high when its population magnitude was far from zero.
With respect to CI coverage, rates were generally within Bradley's criterion range when the random effects were normally distributed and/or the covariance between the random effects was zero.
However, under-coverage occurred under conditions involving nonnormal random effects and, especially, a positive covariance value.
Problems also emerged at the smallest sample sizes, and neither method performed particularly well in terms of CI coverage under nonnormality.
Second, we aimed to replicate the simulation study conducted by Bauer et al. (2006) to evaluate the MC and NA methods to generate confidence intervals in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models.

Both the NA and the MC methods for constructing CIs in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models were not robust to nonnormal random effects.
Indeed, the distribution of the random effects was the factor that exerted the greatest influence on CI coverage rates.
When normality assumptions for the multilevel model do not hold (e.g., random effects are not multivariate normal), then the elements of the ACM that are not well approximated.

Researchers should proceed with caution, checking normality assumptions of the random effects (e.g., an approximate way to do this is to obtain empirical Bayes estimates of the random effects and then test for univariate and multivariate normality) before proceeding to use the methods studied in this manuscript.

We also note that the 1-1-1 multilevel mediation analysis model, as presented, may not be the best model to employ depending on the situation.

Our own position is that the present model may be appropriate for either experimental data where the predictor is manipulated and therefore does not vary on average across clusters, or with cross-sectional clustered data where there is an imbalance in the number of Level 1 units and separation of within-and between-cluster effects is not desired.

In conclusion, we developed and tested code for computing confidence intervals in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models and showed that this approach is feasible in R. Despite the replication of simulation studies being relatively rare, researchers have argued that it is an important endeavor.

We partially replicated the simulation study conducted by Bauer et al. (2006), who evaluated asymptotic normal approximation and Monte Carlo confidence intervals in SAS, whereas our study was conducted in the free, open-source software R. Overall, our results suggest that the proposed R implementation performs adequately in producing confidence intervals for the indirect effect in 1-1-1 multilevel mediation models, and that the main patterns reported by Bauer et al. (2006) can be replicated using an alternative software.
